title: Elysian Health - Tenant Fence & Egress Runway POC scoping
summary: Discovery + POC scoping focused on private connectivity options (VPC peering vs PrivateLink), strict egress controls, region-locking and success metrics for a 6-week pilot. Agreed to run throughput and p99 latency benchmarks against a representative clinical inference workload, validate KMS integration and audit logs, and produce a runbook for regional lockdown + failover. Redwood to propose detailed test matrix and pricing for dedicated reserved capacity during the pilot.
topics: Egress and audit controls (no internet egress, syslogs to customer SIEM)
Workload sizing: 150 concurrent sessions, 200 rps burst
Benchmarks: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, cold KV cache vs warmed cache
Success criteria and timelines (6 week pilot)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on this. We got Owen and Diego from SE to go deep. 
[00:12] Sofia Ramos: Hi! Sofia here. We have Priya and Marcus on to cover security and ops. 
[00:20] Owen Patel: Hey all. Quick agenda: confirm topology, workloads, success criteria, and constraints. 
[00:31] Daniel Kim: We're trying to keep everything in us-east-1, ideally VPC isolated. No cross-region replication unless explicitly approved. 
[00:40] Priya Nambiar: And zero internet egress from inference hosts, logs must go to our Splunk instance via a private endpoint. 
[00:48] Diego Ruiz: Got it. For private connectivity we typically recommend either VPC peering or PrivateLink. Peering is direct route level, PrivateLink gives endpoint-level control but needs endpoint service setup. 
[00:59] Marcus Lee: Performance-wise, which has lower latency? We care about p99s for inference. 
[01:06] Owen Patel: Peering usually has slightly lower hop counts, so marginally lower latency. PrivateLink adds an extra hop through the endpoint, sometimes adds 5-15ms; depends on AZ topology. For our throughput targets it's usually negligible but we'll quantify. 
[01:25] Sofia Ramos: Our SLO target: for the sampled clinical workflow we want p50 < 150ms and p95 < 350ms, p99 < 700ms for 2k token prompts. That may be aggressive, but that's what product wants. 
[01:40] Maya Chen: Ok noted. Can you describe the workload? Concurrent sessions, model sizes? 
[01:47] Daniel Kim: We're planning two classes: real-time triage (short prompts, <256 tokens) about 150 concurrent sessions during day, and batch summarization (8k tokens) that's lower priority but runs nightly. Peak burst 200 rps for short prompts. 
[02:05] Owen Patel: That maps to us recommending a mix of dedicated instances plus a warmed cache strategy. We'll size GPUs for the 8k path separately and configure continuous batching for the short path. 
[02:20] Priya Nambiar: Encryption: all at-rest must be customer-managed keys (CMK) and we need to confirm HSM/KMS integration with our key policies. 
[02:29] Diego Ruiz: Redwood Private supports KMS integrations; for the pilot we can demo using your KMS via a customer-managed key. We'll need an IAM role and some minimal network rules. 
[02:40] Marcus Lee: What about audit logs and retention? We need full request/response audit and 1 year retention, but we may redact PII in logs. 
[02:50] Owen Patel: We stream audit events to a GELF/HTTP endpoint, can also push to S3 with lifecycle. Redaction will be configurable at the SDK/ingestion layer. For the pilot we'll show the event stream into a test Splunk collector. 
[03:05] Sofia Ramos: Cool. Benchmarks — what will you run? 
[03:12] Diego Ruiz: Proposed test matrix: 1) Short prompt steady-state at 150 concurrent: measure throughput and p50/p95/p99; 2) Burst 200 rps spike test for 5 minutes; 3) 8k summarization end-to-end throughput and memory behavior (KV cache warm vs cold); 4) Failover test: region lock + switch to fallback region and validate routing behavior. We'll instrument token-level costs as well. 
[03:40] Daniel Kim: For the failover test, we prefer no automatic cross-region failover during pilot — we want explicit manual failover to validate controls. 
[03:48] Maya Chen: Understood. We'll keep failover manual for the pilot. 
[03:52] Priya Nambiar: Also need to validate PrivateLink's endpoint principal restrictions, and ensure the endpoint policy prevents access from other parties. 
[04:02] Owen Patel: We'll provide sample endpoint policies. 
[04:08] Marcus Lee: Licensing and billing: during the pilot will we be on reserved capacity or pay-as-you-go? 
[04:15] Maya Chen: For the 6-week pilot we recommend a short reserved commitment on Dedicated to guarantee capacity and stable unit economics. We'll send pricing options (monthly pro-rate) for dedicated pools. 
[04:28] Sofia Ramos: Can Redwood run the benchmark inside our account? Or do we need Redwood-managed infra? 
[04:35] Diego Ruiz: Two options: 1) Redwood-managed hosted environment with peered connectivity into your VPC — we control the inference hosts but restrict egress; 2) Private deployment in your VPC (Redwood Private) where the control plane is customer-facing and inference runs inside your network. For the strictest residency and egress controls we usually do Private deployment or Dedicated with PrivateLink. 
[05:00] Daniel Kim: Private deployment sounds safer for compliance, but heavier to stand up. Timeline? 
[05:06] Owen Patel: Typical pilot timeline: week 0-1 prep (network setup, IAM, KMS access), week 2 initial bench runs (short prompts), week 3 heavier 8k tests and failover dry-run, week 4 security validation and log pipeline verification, week 5 tuning and final run, week 6 review and success decision. So ~6 weeks. 
[05:27] Priya Nambiar: Are there open-source or third-party models you support for quantized runs? We may want to test smaller models for cost. 
[05:35] Diego Ruiz: We support a catalog of open models and can test quantized variants. Note that quantization can affect accuracy; Redwood Optimize will provide suggestions per workload. 
[05:48] Sofia Ramos: Success criteria — let's state them now so we're aligned. 
[05:52] Marcus Lee: 1) Functional: no internet egress confirmed, audit events delivered to Splunk, CMK used for all storage. 2) Performance: short prompt p95 < 350ms at 150 concurrent, p99 < 700ms. 3) Throughput: sustains 200 rps burst without failure. 4) Security: SSO/SCIM and RBAC tested for AE accounts. 5) Cost telemetry visible per-token. 
[06:20] Maya Chen: Good. We'll capture those as the POC success criteria. 
[06:24] Daniel Kim: On failover we want the routing rules documented; manual step that triggers fallback, and the TTLs associated. 
[06:31] Owen Patel: We'll produce a runbook. 
[06:34] Sofia Ramos: Any competitors we should be aware of? We're evaluating a few managed vendors. 
[06:39] Priya Nambiar: We're also talking to Anthropic and a smaller infra vendor, name's slipping — maybe CipherWorks. 
[06:46] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll contrast PrivateLink and peering in the doc we send. 
[06:50] [10:12] --- mid-call Q/A and some crosstalk omitted for brevity --- 
[10:25] Diego Ruiz: Network specifics we need from you: VPC CIDR blocks, intended AZs, route table edit permissions, Splunk collector endpoint (private IP/DNS), and the KMS key ARN and trust policy. 
[10:38] Sofia Ramos: we'll share a sanitized network diagram and the key info. 
[10:42] Marcus Lee: For the bench harness, will you bring your own traffic generator or do we instrument ours? 
[10:48] Owen Patel: We can run Redwood's bench harness from within your VPC (agent model) to generate realistic traffic and measure e2e. That avoids internet egress. 
[10:58] Priya Nambiar: Regarding logs we need ability to redact PHI. Does Redwood provide pre-ingest redaction? 
[11:05] Diego Ruiz: Yes, we can configure pre-ingest redaction rules; we'll test with sample payloads. 
[11:12] Sofia Ramos: Ok. Let's talk about test metrics and dashboards. 
[11:16] Hannah Li: From CS we'll provide a dashboard template: p50/p95/p99, token costs, KV cache hit ratio, GPU utilization, and network egress metrics. 
[11:26] Daniel Kim: Cache hit ratio is important; cold starts can blow out latency. We'll want metrics for warmed vs cold. 
[11:33] Owen Patel: We'll include KV cache warm-up scripts as part of the setup. 
[11:37] Maya Chen: Any hard blockers? 
[11:39] Priya Nambiar: One is the KMS policy approval cycle — that can be slow internally. We may need a temporary delegated key for the pilot. 
[11:47] Diego Ruiz: That is common. We can accept a delegated key for pilot then swap to CMK for production. 
[11:53] Marcus Lee: Also a blocker: our security team needs SOC2 type II evidence. 
[11:58] Maya Chen: Redwood has SOC2 and ISO docs; i'll share the security pack and a redacted report. 
[12:05] Sofia Ramos: Timeline wise, if we start prep next week, can we hit the 6 week cadence? 
[12:10] Owen Patel: Yes assuming the KMS and endpoint info arrive within 5 business days. 
[12:14] Daniel Kim: For the benchmark configuration: please include model variants, quantization steps, and expected unit cost per 1k tokens so finance has something to look at. 
[12:24] Diego Ruiz: We'll include a cost sensitivity table. 
[12:28] Maya Chen: Ok let's recap next steps. 
[12:31] Maya Chen: Redwood will: 1) Share pilot test matrix and pricing; 2) Share endpoint policy templates and runbook skeleton; 3) Share SOC2/ISO docs and security pack; 4) Provision bench harness instructions for in-VPC runs. 
[12:48] Sofia Ramos: Elysian will: 1) Share network diagram, KMS ARNs and Splunk endpoint; 2) Make sure SRE has route table permissions for peering if needed; 3) Confirm date for start of week 0. 
[12:59] Priya Nambiar: We'll try to get the KMS delegation approved within three working days. 
[13:05] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll follow up via email and record the action items. Thanks everyone. 
[13:12] Daniel Kim: Thanks all. 
[13:15] [END]
